trivia_fact: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) became generally available in Kubernetes 1.8 (2017). Before RBAC, Kubernetes relied on the simpler ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control) system, which required restarting the API server to change policies — a serious operational headache.

PodSecurityPolicy (PSP) was deprecated in Kubernetes 1.21 and removed in 1.25 after years of being considered too complex and confusing. It was replaced by the simpler Pod Security Admission controller, which uses three predefined levels (Privileged, Baseline, Restricted) instead of custom policies.

ServiceAccounts give pods an identity for API server authentication. Every namespace has a "default" ServiceAccount automatically. Before bound service account tokens (Kubernetes 1.24), SA tokens were non-expiring secrets mounted into every pod — a significant security risk that was quietly exploited in many breaches.

The "default" namespace in Kubernetes is a well-known security anti-pattern. Resources created without specifying a namespace land in "default," leading to mixed workloads, overly broad RBAC rules, and difficulty applying network policies. Production best practice is to never use the default namespace for real workloads.

Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted — a common and dangerous misconception. Anyone with API access to read Secrets sees the plain values after decoding. To get real encryption, you need encryption at rest (EncryptionConfiguration) or an external secret manager like Vault or Sealed Secrets.

Admission controllers are gatekeepers that intercept API requests after authentication and authorization but before persistence. Kubernetes ships with over 30 built-in admission controllers. Mutating admission webhooks (added in 1.9) let you inject sidecars, add labels, or modify resources on the fly — this is how Istio injects its proxy.

etcd stores all Kubernetes cluster state, including Secrets, in plain text by default. Anyone with direct etcd access can read every Secret in the cluster. This is why etcd security (TLS, access control, encryption at rest) is considered the most critical aspect of cluster hardening.

Seccomp (Secure Computing mode) profiles restrict which Linux system calls a container can make. Kubernetes added seccomp support as GA in 1.19. The RuntimeDefault profile blocks about 40 dangerous syscalls while allowing ~300 common ones — a significant attack surface reduction with minimal application impact.

OPA (Open Policy Agent) Gatekeeper is the most popular policy engine for Kubernetes. It uses Rego, a declarative query language, to define policies enforced via admission webhooks. Gatekeeper can prevent deploying images without tags, block privileged pods, enforce resource limits, and hundreds of other organizational policies.

Supply chain security became a major Kubernetes concern after high-profile attacks (SolarWinds, Log4j). The Sigstore project, started by Google and Red Hat in 2021, provides keyless signing and verification for container images. Kubernetes 1.24 added alpha support for verifying signed images via admission policies.
